Newly emerged juvenile Viviparous eelpout (Zoarces viviparus) measure approximately 5.1 cm [Lb = approximately 5.1 cm] in total length at birth, a value that aligns closely with the 51 to 54 millimeter range commonly reported for neonates in wild populations. These diminutive offspring have a correspondingly modest wet weight at birth of 0.46 grams [Wwb = 0.46 grams], reflecting the energetic constraints inherent to lecithotrophic endotrophic larvae that depend exclusively on yolk reserves before shifting to exogenous feeding. The timing of this hatching event is strongly temperature-dependent; at a mean ambient temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the gestation period from fertilisation to eclosion spans approximately 90 days [ab = approximately 90 days], a duration consistent with that observed in other viviparous Zoarcidae inhabiting temperate coastal waters. Some sources indicate a prolonged embryonation period of up to 120 days under similar thermal regimes, but the 90-day figure appears typical for females residing in the Kattegat region. The newly released yolk-sac larvae, or prolarvae, are transparent and exhibit a prominent yolk mass that sustains them through the initial days of free-swimming existence. This relatively small body size at parturition imposes high vulnerability to predation, though it may facilitate rapid incorporation into the demersal juvenile population.

Sexual maturation in Viviparous eelpout occurs at notably different sizes between the sexes, a pattern common among teleosts with moderate sexual dimorphism. Females attain puberty at a total length of 21.5 cm [Lp = 21.5 cm], whereas males become reproductively active at a considerably smaller size of 19 cm [Lp = 19 cm]. The corresponding wet weights at puberty also diverge: females typically weigh 27.4 grams [Wwp = 27.4 grams] at the onset of gonadal maturation, while males achieve puberty at a wet weight of 13.7 grams [Wwp = 13.7 grams], roughly half the female value. This difference likely reflects the greater energetic investment females must make in vitellogenesis and gestation. The age at which the first reproductive event occurs, measured from the time of birth, has been estimated at 265 days after birth [tR = 265 days after birth] when individuals develop under a thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to first spawning is characteristic of a life history strategy that prioritises early reproduction, presumably an adaptation to the seasonal productivity pulses of the North Sea and Baltic Sea ecosystems. After reaching maturity, both sexes continue somatic growth, though at a decelerating rate.

The ultimate sizes attained by adult Viviparous eelpout demonstrate a clear sex-based divergence, with females reaching a larger maximum body length. The female ultimate total length is 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], while the male ultimate total length is 42 cm [Li = 42 cm]. This difference is mirrored in the ultimate wet weights: females achieve a maximum body mass of 510 grams [Wwi = 510 grams], whereas the corresponding male ultimate wet weight is 315 grams [Wwi = 315 grams]. Such dimorphism is typical of species where fecundity is strongly correlated with female body volume, as larger females can accommodate a greater number of developing embryos. Growth proceeds according to a decelerating trajectory; for populations inhabiting the Wadden Sea, where mean water temperatures average 11 °C [T = 11 °C], a von Bertalanffy growth rate of 0.001 per day  has been reported. This relatively slow growth coefficient is consistent with the extended longevity observed under these conditions. The pronounced difference between the ultimate sizes of the sexes suggests that males may allocate a greater proportion of available resources towards reproductive activity at the expense of continued somatic investment.

Longevity in Viviparous eelpout exhibits significant geographic variation that is closely linked to local thermal conditions. In the Wadden Sea, where water temperatures average 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years]. In contrast, populations inhabiting the colder White Sea, characterised by a mean temperature of 4.5 °C [T = 4.5 °C], demonstrate a considerably extended maximum lifespan of 8 years [am = 8 years]. This inverse relationship between temperature and longevity is a well-known pattern among ectothermic vertebrates, likely mediated by reduced metabolic rates and lower cumulative oxidative damage at cooler temperatures. The White Sea fish also exhibit a slower growth trajectory, with a von Bertalanffy growth rate of 0.0006 per day , approximately 40% lower than the rate observed in the Wadden Sea population at a temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This deceleration in both growth and senescence under colder conditions allows individuals to spread their reproductive investment over a longer lifetime. The trade-off between accelerated growth and extended lifespan is evident in these two populations, which occupy opposite ends of the thermal gradient within the species' distributional range.

Reproductive output in Viviparous eelpout scales positively with female body size, as documented in a study conducted in the Kattegat off the coast of Sweden. At a water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a female measuring 20 cm in total body length exhibited a daily reproductive rate of 24 offspring per year [Ri = 24 offspring per year], equivalent to approximately 0.07 eggs per day . At a larger body size of 33 cm, a five-year-old female weighing 153 grams displayed a substantially higher reproductive rate of 125 offspring per year [Ri = 125 offspring per year] under a thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], equivalent to approximately 0.34 eggs per day . This fivefold increase in fecundity with a roughly 60% increase in length underscores the strong selective pressure for continued female growth after puberty. The body weight at a length of 33 cm, recorded as 153 grams , provides a useful reference for allometric scaling relationships within this species. Such size-dependent reproductive rates are typical of iteroparous teleosts where fecundity is ovary-limited and volumetric, and they highlight the critical role that habitat quality and food availability during the growing season play in determining lifetime reproductive success.
